title: A quote handed back as a copy with the same values, refuted on identity alone
summary: The value-object refactor of 190, with `withQuantity` handing back a copy of the quote, for every quantity, instead of the quote it changed. Every field agrees with what 190 hands back; a caller that keeps the quote it passed and the one it got back sees two objects where it saw one. The tool holds the method to `result == q` within each version and refutes it on that alone, the witness replayed on the JVM with the objects' identities.

change.description: `Quote`'s amount, a `long` of cents, becomes a value object, `Money`, so `Quote(long cents, int quantity)` is now `Quote(Money amount, int quantity)`; `Pricing.total` reads `q.amount.cents()` where it read `q.cents`; the pure helper `Pricing.discount` (a tenth off ten items or more) is rewritten as an early return; and the route `POST /quotes` makes the quote with `new Money(cents)`. Nothing is meant to change: not the total, not the event the route sends, not what `Pricing.withQuantity` hands back. In this version `withQuantity` also makes a new quote for one item from `q`'s amount, gives it the quantity, and returns it, after setting `q`'s quantity as before.

risk: Turning a returned argument into a copy is a common defensive edit, and with a value object in the change it looks harmless: the copy has the same amount and quantity. A comparison of returned values field by field passes. Only a caller that relies on getting back the object it passed, and goes on to change one and read the other, sees the difference.
explanation: The run's kernel observations for a Java API method include the identity relation of the result with each object parameter of the result's class, compared within each version as "holds before iff it holds now", never by object ids across versions. Before, `result == q` holds; after, it doesn't. The copy is made for one item and then given the quantity, so that the constructor's refusal of a quantity below 1 doesn't tell the versions apart first: the result's fields and `q`'s agree on every input, and identity is the only observation refuted.
resolution: Hand back `q`, as before, or make the copy the intended change and tell its callers.
notes: Checked by `jvmcontract compare`, which build.py runs as the B9 check of the shop app (`run_tool_compare`): the unpatched build against the patched one, twice under one fresh proof cache, the verdict read from the rerun and the page's output from the first run. The verdict is the subject's; the page lists every other part the run checked.

The joint example of `llm-dlc/loops/foundations.md`'s Phase 5, made an example: the app's sources are the fixture's `before` build (`lib/tests/fixtures/foundations/`), and the patch turns them into its `after` build with the alias-to-copy defect (`defects/alias-to-copy/`) overlaid. `lib/tests/compare.rs` holds `jvmcontract compare` to the same builds inline; this is the same run by build.py, with the app's tests run too.

Nothing in the run is written by hand. The entry points' external inputs (`cents`, `quantity`) are anchored by their observation specs, so no mapping is involved at the boundary. The kernel's relation between the old and new quotes (`old.q.cents == new.q.amount.cents`, `old.q.quantity == new.q.quantity`) is alignment's proposal, inferred from how the two constructors route their parameters into the fields; it stays *proposed*, its evidence the proof under its claim key, and since nothing external anchors a kernel method's inputs, a proved relation there is reported as proved and not as the intended one.

What stays unresolved in every example of the set, by name: `POST /quotes/text` (its string concatenation isn't modeled), `Quote#cents` moved to `Money#cents` (a method of a class the old build doesn't have) and `Quote#quantity`, whose receiver is made differently in the two versions (`Quote(long, int)` before, `Quote(Money, int)` now), which the regression check doesn't relate yet. Before the application-core merge (2026-11-08) it was refused as an instance method instead; the merge's check takes a receiver made by its constructor, of the same construction in both versions.

Run inline on 2026-11-07 (JDK 25.0.5), `jvmcontract compare` on the app compiled unpatched and patched, as build.py compiles it, and on the fixture's builds, with the same verdicts (the times are the fixture's): `Pricing#withQuantity` refuted on `identity:result==q` alone, on `withQuantity(new Quote(new Money(0), 1), 0)`, replayed on a JVM with the objects' identities; `POST /quotes`, `total` and `discount` verified. 0.4 s cold, 0.2 s warm.

`POST /quotes` is an exact hit of 190's proof when run under 190's cache, rightly: the defect changes only `withQuantity`, which the route doesn't reach, so the rewritten builds of the route are 190's (`lib/tests/compare.rs`). Here each example runs under a fresh cache, so it is proved and then reused on the rerun.
The app's tests pass on this version: none keeps the quote it passed.
provenance: Constructed for Phase 5 of `llm-dlc/loops/foundations.md` (the joint example, made an example under the numbers 190-199). Examples 190 to 196 share the refactor: 190 is the refactor alone, and 191 to 196 each add one of the fixture's defects to it.

references.title: Godlin and Strichman, Regression verification: proving the equivalence of similar programs (2013)
Barthe, Crespo and Kunz, Relational verification using product programs (2011)
